concept.name: SQL Query Tuning: Index Seeks, Scans, Clustered & Covering Indexes
concept.tagline: Eliminate slow table scans and high-cost Key Lookups using B-Tree index seeks, clustered primary keys, and composite covering indexes.

spark.summary: Relational query execution hinges on whether the optimizer executes an Index Seek (direct O(log N) B-Tree root-to-leaf traversal) or an Index/Table Scan (O(N) sequential page reads). When non-clustered indexes lack requested SELECT columns, the engine must perform a Key/RID Lookup back to clustered index pages for every row, triggering catastrophic random disk I/O.
spark.keyTakeaway: Eliminate random I/O and table scans by designing clustered indexes on sequential range keys and constructing Covering Indexes (composite keys + INCLUDE columns) that satisfy queries entirely from leaf index pages without touching table data.

concept.whyItMatters: Unindexed or poorly indexed queries degrade from 2ms to 10,000+ms under concurrent traffic, triggering database connection pool exhaustion and 100% CPU spikes. Analyzing execution plans (EXPLAIN ANALYZE) and replacing expensive Key Lookups with covering B-Tree index seeks is the highest-leverage performance optimization in relational databases.
whenToUse: Tables with >100,000 rows where point lookups or range queries suffer from full table scans (Seq Scan).
Queries where execution plans reveal high-cost 'Key Lookup', 'RID Lookup', or 'Bitmap Heap Scan' operations consuming >70% of query time.
High-frequency read APIs where queries can be fulfilled completely by index leaf pages (Covering Index).
Designing primary keys where range scans or time-series sorting align with the physical clustered index order.
whenNotToUse: Small lookup tables (<1,000 rows) where sequential memory page reads are faster than traversing B-Tree branch pages.
Write-heavy tables with high ingestion throughput where maintaining multiple secondary indexes creates severe write amplification and page splits.
Queries returning >20-25% of table rows, where the optimizer's tipping point mathematically favors sequential scans over random single-page lookups.
keyPoints: Clustered Index: Determines the physical sort order of table rows on disk. Leaf nodes are the actual table data pages (e.g. InnoDB clustered primary key). A table can have only one clustered index.
Secondary (Non-Clustered) Index: A separate B-Tree where leaf nodes contain indexed keys plus a row pointer (Clustered Key in MySQL/SQL Server, or physical Tuple ID/RID in PostgreSQL heap tables).
Index Seek vs Index Scan: An Index Seek navigates root-to-leaf via binary search to find exact boundaries in O(log N); an Index Scan reads all leaf pages in sequence in O(N).

Key / RID Lookup (Bookmark Lookup): Occurs when a secondary index seek matches rows, but the query requests additional columns not present in the index, forcing extra random I/O lookups to the clustered index or heap.

Covering Index: Contains all columns needed for a query (in the key or via INCLUDE clause), allowing the database engine to return results entirely from the index tree (Index Only Scan) with zero heap accesses.
Leftmost Prefix Rule: Composite indexes (col1, col2, col3) can only be sought if WHERE clauses filter on leading columns in left-to-right order without skipping.

examples.title: E-Commerce User Order History Tuning
examples.scenario: Querying orders by user_id and created_at with status filter across 40M orders. Existing index was only on created_at, causing a 6-second table scan.
examples.outcome: Added composite covering index on (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (status, total_amount), shifting execution to an Index Only Seek and dropping latency to 1.4ms.

examples.title: FinTech Payment Ledger Bookmark Lookup Elimination
examples.scenario: A secondary index on merchant_id matched 5,000 rows, but required 5,000 Key Lookups to fetch transaction_id, currency, and amount, burning 85% CPU.
examples.outcome: Added INCLUDE (currency, amount) to the secondary index. Eliminated 5,000 random page reads and reduced p99 query latency from 420ms to 2.1ms.

tradeOffs.pro: Covering indexes eliminate heap lookups and deliver sub-millisecond reads.
tradeOffs.con: Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE must update both the table and all secondary B-Tree indexes, increasing write I/O and transaction log volume.

tradeOffs.factor: Clustered Key: Sequential ID vs UUIDv4
tradeOffs.pro: Sequential keys (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT / IDENTITY) append data to the rightmost leaf page with zero page splits.
tradeOffs.con: Random UUIDv4 primary keys cause random disk writes, high B-Tree page splits (50% fill factor), and massive index bloat.

tradeOffs.pro: Index seeks excel when row selectivity is high (<5% of table rows).
tradeOffs.con: When a query matches >15-20% of rows, random single-page lookups cost more than sequential multi-page reads, forcing the optimizer to revert to a full scan.

failureModes.name: Non-SARGable WHERE Expressions
failureModes.description: Wrapping indexed columns in functions (e.g. WHERE DATE(created_at) = '2026-10-13' or WHERE LOWER(email) = ...) prevents the B-Tree from performing an Index Seek, forcing a full index scan.
failureModes.mitigation: Rewrite filters to isolate columns: WHERE created_at >= '2026-10-13 00:00:00' AND created_at < '2026-10-14 00:00:00', or define expression/functional indexes.

failureModes.name: Implicit Type Conversion
failureModes.description: Comparing a VARCHAR column with an integer literal (WHERE account_code = 10492) forces the database to cast every row's string to integer, disabling index seeks.
failureModes.mitigation: Ensure ORM mappings and client queries pass matching parameter data types (WHERE account_code = '10492').

failureModes.name: Over-Indexing & B-Tree Page Splits
failureModes.description: Creating 15+ secondary indexes on a high-concurrency table causes leaf page fragmentation, locks during page splits, and slow write transactions.
failureModes.mitigation: Audit unused indexes using pg_stat_user_indexes or sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats and consolidate overlapping composite indexes.

commonMistakes: Using SELECT * in production queries, which guarantees secondary indexes cannot cover the query and forces costly Key Lookups.

Placing range columns before equality columns in composite indexes: (created_at, user_id) cannot seek efficiently on user_id, whereas (user_id, created_at) allows exact seek on user_id followed by range seek on date.
Believing creating an index on column A and an index on column B is identical to a composite index (A, B) (Bitmap Index Scans are far slower than a single composite B-Tree seek).

deepDive.markdownContent:
## 🔍 Anatomy of SQL Query Execution & B-Tree Navigation

When a database receives a SQL statement, the **Query Optimizer** evaluates candidate execution plans, calculating cost based on estimated page I/O operations and CPU cycles.

### 1. B-Tree Root-to-Leaf Seek Mechanics

A B-Tree index maintains a hierarchical tree where non-leaf pages hold pivot keys pointing to child pages, and leaf pages hold ordered key values with pointers to data.

```text
                  +-------------------+
                  | Root Page (Node)  |
                  | Pivot: [100 | 500]| 
                  +---------+---------+
                           / \  
              +-----------+   +-----------+
              | Branch 1  |   | Branch 2  |
              | [10 | 50] |   | [600|800] |
              +-----+-----+   +-----+-----+
                   /  \            /  \   
        +---------+    +---------+   +---------+
        | Leaf P1 |<-->| Leaf P2 |<->| Leaf P3 | (Doubly Linked List)
        | Keys    |    | Keys    |   | Keys    |
        +---------+    +---------+   +---------+
```

- **Index Seek**: Performs a binary search from the root page down to the leaf page in $O(\log N)$. For a table with 100,000,000 rows, a B-Tree depth of 4 requires reading only 4 8KB pages from the buffer cache to locate the starting row.
- **Index Scan**: Traverses across the horizontal doubly-linked list of leaf pages, reading all $N$ entries in $O(N)$.
- **Table Scan (Seq Scan)**: Discards the index entirely and reads every 8KB data page in the heap from disk.

---

### 2. Clustered Index vs Secondary Index & The Key Lookup Bottleneck

In relational engines (e.g. MySQL InnoDB, Microsoft SQL Server):
1. **Clustered Index**: The table is organized as a B-Tree sorted by the primary key. The leaf pages **are** the data rows containing all table columns.
2. **Secondary Index**: Leaves contain the indexed column values plus the **Clustered Key** (or heap Row ID / TID in PostgreSQL).

```text
[Query: SELECT order_id, status, total_amount FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 42]

SCENARIO A: Secondary Index on (customer_id) [WITHOUT Covering Columns]
1. Index Seek on idx_customer_id finds 50 matching leaf entries.
2. For EACH of the 50 rows, the engine must perform a KEY LOOKUP:
   Navigate the Clustered Index B-Tree (3-4 page reads each) to fetch 'total_amount'.
   Total Page Reads: 4 (Index Seek) + (50 * 3 Random Lookups) = 154 Page Reads!

SCENARIO B: Covering Composite Index on (customer_id) INCLUDE (status, total_amount)
1. Index Seek on idx_customer_covering finds 50 matching leaf entries.
2. All requested columns (order_id, status, total_amount) exist in the leaf page!
3. Engine returns data directly without touching the clustered index or heap.
   Total Page Reads: 4 Page Reads! (97.4% reduction in I/O)
```

---

### 3. The Composite Index Design Rule: Equality First, Range Second

To maximize index seek selectivity on queries with multiple filters:
1. Place **Equality (`=`)** columns first in the composite index.
2. Place **Range (`>`, `<`, `BETWEEN`, `IN`)** columns last among the seek keys.
3. Include columns needed for projection in the `INCLUDE` clause (or at the end of the index) to avoid making the index tree wider.

```sql
-- BAD INDEX: Range column first
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_bad ON orders (created_at, customer_id);
-- Query cannot seek on customer_id because the B-Tree is sorted primarily by created_at!
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 99 AND created_at >= '2026-10-01';

-- GOOD INDEX: Equality first, Range second, Covered columns included
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_good ON orders (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (status, total_amount);
-- Engine performs an exact binary seek to customer_id = 99, then a range scan on created_at!
```

caseStudy.problem: Merchant admin orders table (85M rows) suffered 8,000ms query timeouts during Black Friday sales due to full table scans and Key Lookups.
caseStudy.solution: Restructured primary key clustering and deployed composite covering indexes with INCLUDE clauses on high-QPS filter paths.
caseStudy.impact: Query latency dropped from 8,200ms to 2.1ms (99.97% drop), DB CPU utilization decreased from 92% to 18% under 40k QPS.

relationships.description: Database indexing establishes core B-Tree vs LSM-Tree mechanics; SQL query tuning applies B-Tree seeks, scans, and covering index structures to optimize production relational queries.

SQL covering indexes achieve sub-5ms latency inside the database engine without cache invalidation complexity, whereas in-memory caches achieve sub-millisecond QPS at the cost of external RAM and cache-aside state management.
Sharding distributes tables horizontally across instances, but single-node partition performance remains fundamentally governed by clustered and covering index design.

questions.title: Diagnosing Key Lookup vs Index Only Scan in Execution Plans
questions.prompt: In an execution plan for a query filtering on a secondary index, you observe an Index Seek followed by an expensive 'Key Lookup' (or 'Bookmark Lookup') consuming 85% of total query operator cost. What is the root cause and the most efficient resolution?

options.text: The table statistics are outdated; running ANALYZE TABLE will automatically convert the query to an Index Only Scan without index changes.
options.explanation: Statistics describe data distribution but cannot provide missing column data that is physically absent from secondary index leaf pages.

options.text: The secondary index satisfies the WHERE condition but lacks columns referenced in the SELECT clause, forcing the engine to fetch row data from the clustered index for each matching row. Solution: Add the missing projected columns to the index as key or INCLUDE columns (Covering Index).
options.explanation: Correct! Key Lookups occur whenever a non-clustered index does not cover all columns requested in the query. Expanding the index into a covering index eliminates the lookups.

options.text: The primary key is corrupted; rebuilding the clustered index with DROP and RECREATE will eliminate secondary lookups.
options.explanation: Key lookups are normal behavior for non-covering queries, not a sign of index corruption.

options.text: The database engine has exceeded max_connections and downgraded the execution plan to sequential I/O.
options.explanation: Connection limits affect client concurrency, not optimizer index covering decisions.

rubric.excellent: Identifies that missing projected columns trigger secondary-to-clustered random I/O lookups and prescribes a covering index with INCLUDE columns.
rubric.acceptable: Recognizes that the index is missing columns required by the query.
rubric.gap: Confuses key lookups with table corruption or outdated query statistics.

questions.sampleSolution: A Key Lookup occurs when an index seek satisfies query predicates but fails to provide columns in the SELECT projection. Creating a covering index (CREATE INDEX idx_name ON table (where_cols) INCLUDE (select_cols)) allows an Index Only Scan, dropping I/O to zero heap accesses.
questions.explanation: By storing unindexed projection columns in the leaf level of the index via INCLUDE, the engine resolves the query entirely within the index B-Tree.

interviewProblems.title: Architect High-QPS Multi-Tenant Query Indexing Under High Concurrency
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: You are the Principal Database Architect for a multi-tenant SaaS ledger processing 10,000 queries per second on a table with 200,000,000 rows. A critical endpoint executes: SELECT transaction_id, created_at, status, amount FROM ledger WHERE tenant_id = ? AND status IN ('PENDING', 'FAILED') AND created_at >= ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50. Currently, the query takes 3,500ms and causes 100% database CPU. How do you design the clustered index, composite secondary indexes, and query structure to guarantee sub-5ms p99 latency?
constraints: Zero downtime allowed during index deployment

dimensions.name: Composite Index Key Ordering
dimensions.description: Applying equality-before-range rules to minimize B-Tree leaf scan volume.

dimensions.name: Covering Index & Key Lookup Elimination
dimensions.description: Eliminating random page reads for projected columns (amount, transaction_id).

dimensions.name: Production Operational Safety
dimensions.description: Zero-downtime online index builds without table write locks.

interviewProblems.sampleDefense: 1. Index Design: Create a composite covering index: CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_ledger_tenant_status_date ON ledger (tenant_id, status, created_at DESC) INCLUDE (amount, transaction_id). Leading tenant_id provides exact partition seek. status IN (...) performs bounded range seeks. created_at DESC aligns perfectly with ORDER BY created_at DESC, eliminating in-memory sorting. INCLUDE (amount, transaction_id) satisfies SELECT completely, yielding an Index Only Scan with zero Key Lookups. 2. Operational Safety: Deploy via CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY (or ALGORITHM=INPLACE in MySQL) to prevent exclusive table locks, avoiding transaction pool starvation. 3. Result: B-Tree depth traversal requires 4 page reads, scanning at most 50 leaf entries, executing in <2ms directly from buffer cache.
commonPitfalls: Placing created_at as the leading column, forcing a scan across all tenants
Omitting amount from the index, causing 50 random Key Lookups per query
Running standard CREATE INDEX without CONCURRENTLY, causing full table write locks
